Transcriptomic analysis reveals that Gp53 alters the expression of 3,342 genes, including genes involved in cell division and virulence-associated processes. DNA-binding assays demonstrate that Gp53 directly represses promoters of key host genes, including ftsZ , fleQ , pslA , and amrZ . Gp53-mediated repression of ftsZ disrupts Z-ring formation and inhibits cell division, while ftsZ expression restores these defects. Structural and mutational analyses identify residues important for Gp53-DNA interaction. Together, these findings reveal a phage-encoded mechanism that coordinately interferes with bacterial cell division and virulence-associated pathways, providing mechanistic insights into host transcriptional regulation during phage infection and expanding our understanding of phage-host interactions.

title: Chromogranin A-phosphatidic acid association coordinates late stages of regulated exocytosis
abstract: Chromogranin A is a major component of secretory granules that contributes to granule biogenesis, cargo organization and regulated secretion in neuroendocrine cells. We previously identified a phosphatidic acid (PA)-binding domain (PABD) within CgA that promotes secretory granule formation by remodeling trans -Golgi network membranes. Here, we investigate whether this lipid-protein association also contributes to the late stages of regulated exocytosis. Using fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy combined with Förster resonance energy transfer, we find that CgA undergoes a stimulation-dependent association with PA at exocytic sites in living cells. Immunofluorescence and electron microscopy further show that CgA remains transiently associated with fused secretory granule membranes. Functional analyses reveal that disruption of the PABD alters secretory granule exocytosis by accelerating CgA release, modifying quantal catecholamine release and fusion pore dynamics, and changing the early kinetics of secretory granule membrane retrieval. Together, these findings support a model in which the CgA/PA association is not restricted to secretory granule biogenesis but also contributes to the temporal coordination of multiple post-fusion events during regulated secretion. This work identifies a lipid-protein interaction that links distinct stages of the secretory granule life cycle in neuroendocrine cells.

title: Single-cell chromatin maps of thymic carcinoma reveal a conserved malignant state and its immunosuppressive dependencies
abstract: Thymic carcinoma is a rare and aggressive malignancy with limited therapeutic options. Although recent single-cell transcriptomic studies have begun to resolve its cellular composition, its regulatory landscape remains poorly characterized. We present a single-cell chromatin accessibility resource comprising 26,661 high-quality nuclei from three tumors and two adjacent normal tissues, with annotated malignant and immune populations, cell-type-resolved peaks, and gene activity estimates. To illustrate its utility, exploratory analyses identified a recurrent tumor cluster, T3, in all three tumors examined, with shared accessibility at therapeutically relevant loci, including KIT , FGFR3 , and SYK , and an inferred regulatory program involving ELF2 , BCLAF1 , PBX3 , IKZF1 , NFKB1 , TFDP2 , and POU2AF1 , alongside exhaustion-associated CD8⁺ T-cell and M2-like macrophage chromatin programs. Given the cohort size, these observations are descriptive and hypothesis-generating. This resource provides a foundation for future functional and translational studies of thymic carcinoma.

title: A dielectric spectroscopic measurement of single Saccharomyces pastorianus growth and heat-shock response
abstract: Cell growth and heat shock response (HSR) are central to cellular adaptation, fate determination, and survival under fluctuating environments, yet their continuous quantification in individual suspended microbial cells remains challenging. Here, we present microwave dielectric spectroscopic cytometry (DiSC) for real-time, label-free monitoring of single-cell growth and HSR in budding yeast, Saccharomyces pastorianus , under physiological culture conditions. Integrated optical microscopy enabled simultaneous tracking of morphological dynamics during growth, heat shock, and apoptosis. At 32 °C, cells exhibited continuous biomass accumulation with fluctuating growth rates but relatively conserved molecular composition profiles (MCPs). Upon heat shock (from 32 °C to 42 °C), cells displayed discontinuous biomass accumulation, rapid mass fluctuations, and dynamically varying MCPs across all 17 cells analyzed. A subset of cells subsequently underwent apoptotic collapse, with onset times ranging from ~ 20 min during temperature ramping to more than 60 min at 42 °C or remaining absent throughout the 340 min observation window, revealing pronounced cell-to-cell heterogeneity. Post-apoptotic cells exhibited stabilized MCP dynamics. Analyses of two- to four-cell lineages further demonstrated divergent apoptotic outcomes among closely related progeny. These results establish DiSC as a promising platform for continuous single-cell quantification of growth, stress adaptation, and phenotypic heterogeneity while highlighting opportunities for further improvements in system performance and analytical capability.

title: Transient hemispheric lateralization is associated with intensity-dependent aftereffects of low-frequency rTMS
abstract: Low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) can alter brain activity during and after stimulation, but the relationship between these immediate responses and subsequent effects remains unclear. In a randomized, single-blind crossover design, twenty healthy adults receive 1 Hz rTMS over the left motor cortex at sham, 80%, 100%, and 120% of resting motor threshold (RMT). electroencephalography (EEG) is recorded before, during, and after rTMS. Stimulation at and above threshold elicits robust transient responses, characterized by enhanced TMS-evoked potentials, increased beta-band power, increased beta-band lateralization and recruited bilateral cortical activities. Also, they induce significant aftereffect with a decrease in hemispheric lateralization after rTMS. Mediation analyses links stimulation intensity to this subsequent rebalancing through transient beta-band lateralization. In an exploratory stroke cohort, lower beta-band lateralization is associated with better motor function. These findings suggest that low-frequency rTMS induces intensity-dependent transient responses and aftereffects. Transient beta-band lateralization is associated with subsequent interhemispheric rebalancing and may serve as a marker for optimizing personalized neurorehabilitation.

title: An ensemble framework for robust drug response prediction and large-scale sensitivity profiling across cancers
abstract: Predicting how cancers respond to treatment remains difficult because tumors are diverse and computational models often perform poorly on unfamiliar drugs or samples. Here we show that the accuracy of deep learning models varies across molecular inputs, drug descriptions, model designs, and evaluation settings, with the largest losses when models are tested on previously unseen drugs or distinct datasets. We therefore develop Drug Response Integration and Voting Ensemble, a meta-learning framework that combines models using predictions from held-out data. A nine-model ensemble improves predictive accuracy, drug ranking, and stability over individual models and ensemble approaches. We implement the framework as a reproducible Nextflow workflow and use it to build a resource of measured and predicted drug responses across cancer cell lines, patient-derived samples, and compound libraries. In colorectal cancer, the framework identifies treatments with confirmed antitumor activity in cell and animal models. This approach provides a scalable strategy for therapeutic discovery.

title: DNMT1 function in cortical PV interneurons modulates cortical network activity, mood disorder‑related behavior, and perineuronal nets
abstract: Parvalbuminergic (PV) interneurons are central to cortical network stability and psychiatric vulnerability. Here, we identify DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1) as a key epigenetic regulator linking PV interneuron function to glial and extracellular matrix remodeling. Conditional PV-specific Dnmt1 deletion, combined with single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq), snATAC-seq, in vivo electrophysiology, histology, and behavioral analyses, revealed that DNMT1 loss increases PV spiking but reduces inhibitory efficacy, driving network desynchronization and depression- and anxiety-like behavior in mice. These physiological changes were accompanied by non-cell-autonomous transcriptional and chromatin alterations, affecting perineuronal net (PNN) organization and neuron-glia communication. Cell-cell communication analyses predicted reorganized perisomatic signaling, and compartmental modeling of oligodendrocyte lineage dynamics further revealed impaired formation of PNN-supporting perineuronal oligodendrocytes, consistent with a tissue-level reduction in PNN integrity. Together, our findings demonstrate that DNMT1 maintains inhibitory circuit stability through PV interneuron function, secondarily shaping glial states and extracellular scaffolds to support cortical network synchronization and affective behavior.

title: Autophagy regulates the hepatic protein acetylation through modulating acetyl-CoA metabolite
abstract: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) are essential for hepatic protein function and signaling. While autophagy regulates the hepatic proteome through degradation and transcriptional control, its role in PTMs remains unclear. Using genetic and pharmacological models, we show that autophagy deficiency causes protein accumulation with increased ubiquitination, SUMOylation, methylation, and phosphorylation, but markedly reduces global protein acetylation—the hepatic acetylome—which is enhanced by autophagy activation. This acetylation loss results from decreased hepatic acetyl-CoA levels, independent of acetyltransferase or deacetylase expression. Mechanistically, NRF2 activation suppresses key acetyl-CoA biosynthetic enzymes (Acly, Acss, Mlycd, Pdha1), limiting substrate availability. Acetyl-CoA or acetate supplementation restores the protein acetylation and alleviates liver injury and inflammation in autophagy-deficient models. Similar reductions in acetylation and acetyl-CoA enzyme expression occur in preclinical models and human chronic liver disease. These findings identify a role for autophagy in regulating the hepatic protein acetylation through metabolic control of acetyl-CoA, with potential therapeutic implications.

title: A telomere-to-telomere reference genome for Rosa roxburghii reveals lineage-specific diversification of triterpenoid biosynthesis
abstract: Rosa roxburghii ( RRT ) is a nutritionally and medicinally important Rosaceae species that accumulates diverse bioactive compounds, making it an excellent system for investigating the genetic basis and evolutionary diversification of specialized metabolism. Here, we report a complete telomere-to-telomere (T2T), gap-free genome assembly of the elite cultivar ‘Guinong No. 5’ ( RRT5 ), comprising 494.57 Mb with a contig N50 of 51.44 Mb and a base accuracy of over 99.99%. Of this assembly, 99.9% were anchored to seven pseudo-chromosomes. Multi-omics analyses identified OSC , CYP , and UGT genes potentially involved in triterpenoid biosynthesis, while gene–metabolite correlation analyses highlighted MYB30 and MYB31 as candidate regulators of multiple triterpenoids. Notably, the biosynthetic capacities for Kaji-ichigoside F1 and rosamultin vary across lineages within Rosoideae, likely reflecting lineage-specific gene gain or loss and/or evolutionary divergence in regulatory pathways. Together, the RRT5 genome, transcriptome, and profiling of the eight key triterpenoids provide a valuable resource for elucidating triterpenoid biosynthesis, regulation, and evolution, and for guiding genome-informed breeding of R. roxburghii .

title: Long-term malaria exposure in pathogen-endemic environments is associated with distinct immune states
abstract: Long-term exposure to malaria may shape baseline immune function, yet its effects in healthy adults remain unclear. Here we show that healthy Kenyan adults living in regions with higher malaria transmission and broader infectious exposure have distinct baseline immune profiles. Using blood-cell gene expression and circulating immune mediators from 60 adults across regions with differing malaria endemicity, we identify 658 differentially expressed genes. Higher exposure is associated with increased expression of pathways related to B-cell activation, antigen presentation, immune regulation, and post-transcriptional RNA processing, alongside reduced inflammatory, chemotactic, and vascular gene programmes. Circulating immune mediators are modestly elevated despite reduced inflammatory gene expression, indicating a partial dissociation between systemic mediator levels and cellular transcription. Our findings show that long-term malaria exposure in pathogen-endemic environments is associated with a distinct immune state characterised by adaptive immune activation and restrained inflammatory transcription, which may influence responses to subsequent infections and vaccination.

title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals early immune responses in HIV and tuberculosis coinfection in humanized mice
abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) coinfection is a major public health concern, yet early immune and tissue changes during coinfection remain incompletely understood. Here we show, using a humanized mouse model and spatial transcriptomics of lung tissue, that early immune cell infiltration differs across single and combined infections. Mtb infection is associated with increased CD4 positive T cell infiltration, whereas this response is reduced in HIV infection and coinfection. Coinfected lungs also show lower natural killer cell abundance. Spatial profiling identifies distinct airway regions with different immune cell compositions and a lymphoid aggregate in coinfected lung with a distinct transcriptional profile. Although this aggregate lacks the cellular organization of a mature granuloma, it exhibits granuloma-associated gene expression signatures and pathways related to reactive oxygen species production, oxidative phosphorylation, transforming growth factor beta signaling, and interferon signaling. These findings define early spatial immune changes associated with coinfection.

title: Neural oscillations and network specialisation in early childhood captured with next-generation magnetoencephalography
abstract: Early childhood sees very rapid brain development, reflected in substantial alterations in neural oscillations and reorganisation of functional networks. Yet, these developmental trajectories remain poorly understood, due to a paucity of studies in this age range. Optically pumped magnetometer-based magnetoencephalography provides a unique opportunity to assess neural activity from young children with high spatiotemporal resolution. Here, we use this technology to determine the development of neural oscillations and functional networks in 111 children aged 1–5 years, including both cross-sectional and longitudinal data (163 datasets). We demonstrate that the aperiodic slope and offset increase across this age range, with regional specificity: the greatest changes were shown in temporo-parietal regions. Periodic power shifted towards higher frequencies, such that theta oscillations decreased with age, while alpha and beta increased. Global connectivity decreased from 1–5 years, driven by a broadband bilateral parietal and frontal network, while task-relevant occipital connections increased with age. Our findings establish that oscillatory power and connectivity patterns evolve significantly over early childhood, contributing foundational information for understanding the neural underpinnings of maturing cognitive abilities.

title: Differential excitatory-inhibitory balance within dorsolateral prefrontal cortex links inter-network interactions in working memory
abstract: Working memory involves complex activity and interactions across multiple brain areas. However, little is known about how these large-scale activity and interaction patterns relate to resting-state activity and to excitatory and inhibitory interactions within localized brain regions. Here we show, using multimodal neuroimaging and large-scale neural network modelling, that excitatory and inhibitory neuronal activities within the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) are linked to inter-network interactions during working memory. We generate testable predictions by perturbing a resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)-constrained neural network model and by performing molecular-enriched analyses using fMRI and positron emission tomography (PET) receptor maps. We then show that frontoparietal and default-mode network activity, which differs between resting state and working memory, covaries with DLPFC activity and its functional interactions with these networks. These findings provide a mechanistic account of how local excitatory and inhibitory activity may support large-scale network dynamics involved in working memory.

title: Immune checkpoint blockade activates macrophages and remodels the lymph node microenvironment in melanoma metastasis
abstract: The factors that drive therapeutic resistance and variable patient response to immune checkpoint blockade therapies within the metastatic lymph nodes are poorly understood. Activation of lymph node immune cells is associated with effective immune checkpoint blockade responses or alternately enforce immunosuppression. Here we investigate a murine model of lymph node melanoma metastasis that is amenable to combination immune checkpoint blockade at the cellular, protein, and transcriptional level. Checkpoint blockade spatially reorganizes and activates T and B lymphocytes as well as lymph node stromal cells. Notably, myeloid cells, key mediators of lymph node immune function, are reprogrammed to an immunostimulatory phenotype upon checkpoint blockade. Our findings in this murine lymph node metastasis system support a model in which immunostimulatory macrophages are induced and macrophage-mediated T cell suppression is released during effective immunotherapy.

title: A modular constitutive single-plasmid platform for efficient production of a recombinant Strep A glycoconjugate vaccine
abstract: Production of glycoconjugate vaccines has long relied upon chemical methods which are highly complex and expensive, resulting in vaccines that are not widely affordable. Heterologous bioconjugation methods, such as Protein-Glycan Coupling Technology (PGCT), have emerged as a path to significantly cheaper manufacture using safe host organisms, such as Escherichia coli , for recombinant glycoconjugate expression. PGCT glycoconjugate synthesis components are typically encoded across three plasmids and require the addition of exogenous chemical inducers for gene expression. In this study, we utilise modular DNA assembly to generate a single constitutive plasmid for biosynthesis of a Streptococcus pyogenes rhamnose polysaccharide glycoconjugate vaccine. This approach resulted in a greater than seven-fold glycoconjugate yield as well as simplified cell culture conditions compared to the traditional three plasmid inducible system. Importantly, given the modular nature of this method, this innovation could be applied to the manufacture of glycoconjugate vaccines against a range of pathogens.

title: Suppression of follistatin by spontaneous seizures dysregulates neurogenesis in a model of Alzheimer’s disease neuropathology
abstract: Adult hippocampal neurogenesis is perturbed in neurological disorders accompanied by seizures, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD). The molecular mechanisms by which seizures disrupt neurogenesis are unclear. Here, we report that follistatin (FST), an antagonist of TGFβ ligands, plays a pivotal role in seizure-induced dysregulation of neurogenesis. We find that FST expression is reduced in the dentate gyrus of a mouse model of AD neuropathology that exhibits infrequent spontaneous seizures similar to those in individuals with AD. Treatment with an antiseizure drug improves FST expression in AD mice, whereas a seizure-inducing agent suppresses FST expression in wild-type mice. We identify c-Fos, whose expression is suppressed by the seizure-induced transcription factor ∆FosB, as a transcriptional activator of Fst . Lastly, ablation of Fst dysregulates neurogenesis dynamics in wild-type mice, whereas FST treatment normalizes dynamics in AD mice. These findings reveal a previously unidentified activity-dependent mechanism in which the expression of FST controls neurogenesis dynamics.

title: Human iPSC-derived motor neurons with TDP-43 nuclear loss present early ALS pathological phenotypes
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a complex neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive loss of motor neurons and presents a critical need for effective treatments. To investigate the impact of TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) nuclear depletion in ALS, we established and characterized a human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neuron model carrying a mutation that disrupts TDP-43 nuclear localization. The model successfully recapitulates functional deficits observed in ALS patients, including impaired neurite outgrowth, reduced axonal regeneration, and neuronal hyperexcitability. Proteomic and metabolomic profiling revealed early mechanisms underlying ALS neuronal pathophysiology, involving altered oxidative stress and neurotransmitter release. TDP-43 nuclear depletion led to mis-splicing STMN2 and KCNQ2 , defects characteristic of TDP-43-associated disease. Notably, a splice-switching antisense oligonucleotide successfully restored normal STMN2 splicing and function, demonstrating that directly correcting splicing defects can rescue motor neurons. This work provides a comprehensive understanding of TDP-43 nuclear depletion in the context of ALS pathogenesis and offers potential targets for RNA-targeted therapeutic intervention, pointing towards the development of precision medicine approaches and early diagnostic markers for ALS.

title: Cellular and spatial context of genetic convergence between insomnia liability and DTI ALPS perivascular diffusivity
abstract: Sleep has been linked to brain waste clearance and glymphatic/perivascular transport, yet whether insomnia shares genetic architecture with perivascular diffusivity remains unclear. Here we show that insomnia liability and diffusion tensor imaging measures along the perivascular space have little genome-wide genetic correlation but converge locally at chromosome 17q21.31. Polygenic enrichment, conjunctional false discovery rate, and Bayesian colocalization analyses support shared statistical signals in this region, which contains the MAPT inversion locus. Transcriptome-wide, gene-level fine-mapping, and summary-data Mendelian randomization analyses prioritize HEXIM1 , ACBD4 , EFTUD2 , and MAPT . Tissue, cell-type, spatial transcriptomic, and sleep-perturbation analyses place these candidates in neuronal, glial, immune, vascular, and perivascular contexts, with effects varying by brain region and imaging phenotype. Together, these findings support localized genetic convergence rather than a genome-wide shared architecture and provide biological context for future studies of perivascular imaging phenotypes and neurodegeneration-related processes.

title: Non‑monotonic reorganization of cortical neuron firing despite ongoing delta‑dominated activity
abstract: Delta - dominated activity is a hallmark of anesthesia and non‑REM sleep, yet how neuronal firing evolves across these rhythms remains unclear. Here, by tracking cortical neuron firing in the ketamine‑xylazine model, we find that across continuing delta - dominated activity, population firing rates progress through successive epochs of excitation, suppression, and re - emergence. Concurrently, fine‑scale spike timing and burst dynamics exhibit non - monotonic modulation, revealing continuous reorganization beneath the ongoing delta-dominated oscillation. At the transition to theta - dominated activity, a restructuring of temporal patterning without a significant shift in the firing - rate distribution suggests that temporal structure, rather than firing rate, defines this transition. These population - level dynamics were firing - rate - dependent: high‑firing - rate neurons were more tightly modulated, whereas low‑firing-rate neurons exhibited more heterogeneous changes. Neither ketamine nor xylazine alone recapitulates these dynamics, suggesting their combined action creates a uniquely dynamic architecture. These findings reveal a continuous, firing - rate - dependent reorganization of single-neuron activity during ongoing delta-dominated states.

title: Linking centromere stretch to SAC signaling in mammalian oocytes with insights from modified kinetochore model
abstract: The spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) monitors kinetochore-microtubule interactions to ensure accurate chromosome segregation. In mitosis, investigation of its silencing at anaphase centers on whether attachment or tension is the key signal, while in meiosis for mammalian oocytes it remains unclear whether centromere stretching contributes to SAC deactivation, because in this reductional division sister chromatids co-segregate during meiosis I. While previous studies have linked bivalent tension to SAC control in oocytes, this measurement cannot be directly equated with mitotic chromatin stretching. Here, by tagging the N-terminus of NDC80/HEC1, we developed a mouse oocyte model that features stable microtubule attachments, yet exhibits persistent SAC signaling at metaphase I. Our comprehensive analysis reveals a strong correlation between centromere stretching and SAC signaling. Furthermore, high-resolution live imaging demonstrates that these modified kinetochores impair their oscillatory movements, a process vital for error correction, while chromosome congression remains largely unaffected. Collectively, our data suggest that stable microtubule attachment alone is insufficient to silence SAC in mammalian oocytes; instead, centromere stretching may serve as a critical signal to deactivate the checkpoint. These findings underscore the adaptability of core cell-cycle surveillance pathways.

title: Frequency-specific oscillations track parallel processing of linguistic structural and lexical-semantic information from perception to decision
abstract: The ability to perceive linguistic features is essential for language comprehension, yet how our brains dynamically recognize, integrate and process distinct linguistic features is still controversial. Here, we employ magnetoencephalography to examine the spatiotemporal organization of two word-level dimensions: syllabic structural and lexical-semantic regularities using a novel auditory linguistic task with an orthogonal design. During the recognition of linguistic features, we identify time-dependent and frequency-specific oscillations in temporal-frontal, para-hippocampal, parietal areas, supporting neural dynamics spanning from linguistic to memory and decision-making processing. Decoding linguistic features in timeseries reveals parallel activities of structure and lexical semantics through distinct neural networks, which beyond the language network extending from auditory cortex to language–sensorimotor hubs. By linking behavior to neural responses, we uncover the frontal-parietal network associated with individual differences in response to dual-feature violations. Overall, our findings reveal the concurrent availability of structural and lexical-semantic representation and characterize task-specific choice tendency under dual-feature conflict.

title: Time-locked activities of resting-state networks that transiently occur in human resting-state brain activities
abstract: Spontaneous brain activities at rest are organized into resting-state networks, such as the default mode network. While the default mode network is assumed to interact with other networks to integrate distributed information, its fine-scale temporal dynamics remain unclear. Here, we demonstrate how the default mode network interacts with other networks at millisecond-scale temporal resolution. Using a large dataset of resting-state magnetoencephalography and our recently proposed method, we estimated the spatiotemporal patterns that recur in resting-state brain activity and then examined the interactions across the resting-state networks in these patterns. In the alpha/beta band component of the spatiotemporal patterns, the default mode network and the visual/sensorimotor network alternately appear with a lag of about 24/13 ms, corresponding to about π /2 rad in the alpha/beta oscillation. These alternating and orthogonal activities of the resting-state networks may reflect the brain’s strategy to achieve both the integration and separation of visual and sensorimotor information via the default mode network. Furthermore, we reveal how these activities consecutively move between the default mode network and the visual/sensorimotor network in tens of milliseconds. They move in different ways depending on their direction, suggesting that distinct mechanisms generate the movements in different directions.

title: MUFASA: a continuous-time stochastic framework for realistic fluorescence microscopy simulation
abstract: We present MUFASA ( M ulti-Protocol U nified F luorescence-based A dvanced S imulation A lgorithm), a physically grounded, continuous-time simulator of several super-resolution fluorescence microscopy protocols. By modeling fluorophore dynamics using continuous-time Markov chains, MUFASA’s simulation features yield realistic photon emission behavior across both Single Molecule Localization Microscopy (SMLM) and fluorescence fluctuation-based (FF-SRM) settings–independently of frame duration and sampling. The framework supports both individual emitters and structure-level simulations, incorporating photophysical transitions, photobleaching, and camera properties.To quantitatively compare simulations with real data, we introduce a novel validation metric based on the 1-Wasserstein distance between simulated and experimental photon-count distributions. Another functionality of MUFASA is the estimation of key photophysical parameters (e.g., molar extinction coefficient) and the suggestion of optimal light-source power ranges from fluctuation data.An intuitive Python-based graphical interface for real-time parameter tuning, visualization, and TIFF export is provided.Designed for biologists, physicists, microscopists, and computational imaging engineers, MUFASA offers a practical platform for microscopy experiment design, hypothesis testing and holds the potential of being used for the generation of realistic training data for data-driven methods across modalities.

title: Machine learning analysis of cilia driven particle transport distinguishes primary ciliary dyskinesia from normal cilia
abstract: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is a genetic condition causing dysmotile cilia and abnormal mucociliary clearance. Despite advances in understanding disease pathogenesis, diagnosis remains challenging. Here, we show that machine learning analysis of cilia-driven particle transport can objectively detect primary ciliary dyskinesia-related dysfunction. Using high-speed video microscopy, we captured fluorescent microsphere movement on cultured multiciliated cells from 14 individuals with primary ciliary dyskinesia and 10 healthy donors (602 videos). We developed CiliaTracks, an open-source computational framework that extracts measures of micropsphere movement, visualizes transport patterns, and classifies cilia-propelled particle transport. Quantitative and visual analyses reveal distinct motility profiles between PCD and non-primary ciliary dyskinesia and normal recordings. Classical machine learning models and a convolutional neural network classify recordings with 95-97% accuracy and differentiate affected from normal samples. Machine learning provides an objective, accurate framework for characterizing ciliary dysfunction, offering potential as a diagnostic tool for primary ciliary dyskinesia.

title: Balancing energy efficiency and functional demand via bimodal coupling optimization in biological rhythms
abstract: Biological rhythms are governed by intricate interactions among oscillatory subsystems, yet how they balance functional demands and energy efficiency remains unclear. We present a bimodal coupling optimization strategy where physiological systems alternate between synchronized (energy-saving) and desynchronized (function-priority) coupling modes. Using the water-filling principle developed in communications engineering, we derive necessary optimality conditions showing that energy-efficiency (oxygen uptake per cardiac work) maximization requires synchronized heart rate(HR)-respiration oscillations. Then, system modeling confirms task/stress-induced oxygen demands enhance oxygen uptake at the cost of desynchronization and reduced efficiency. Experiments reveal a 70.36% decrease in HR-respiration synchronization during arithmetic versus relaxation, enabling 4.43% higher oxygen uptake but with 11.38% lower energy efficiency. This bimodal coupling optimization strategy is also evident in pancreatic islets, with their insulin/glucagon oscillator alternating between in-phase (energy-saving) and anti-phase (rapid glucose reduction) coupling. This framework, integrating engineering and life sciences, reveals a universal regulatory principle for biological oscillatory systems.

title: Self-regulated emergence of heavy-tailed weight distributions in evolving complex network architectures
abstract: The nervous system continuously adjusts connection strengths and reorganizes its structure to form and maintain complex connectivity patterns with heavy-tailed weight distributions. We propose a parsimonious model in which structural and synaptic plasticity are driven by common diffusion dynamics. Synaptic plasticity alone generates heavy-tailed weight distributions, but only when activity spreading remains predominantly local. However, when combined with structural plasticity through adaptive rewiring, the model also generates these distributions with more extensive activity flow. Furthermore, adaptive rewiring produces complex network structures with convergent-divergent circuits. These circuits contain motifs that are pervasive in nervous systems and are responsible for context-sensitive signal propagation and enhanced signal-to-noise ratios. Our model robustly reproduces these results across diverse dynamical regimes while capturing key connectivity features of both C. elegans and mouse brain networks. These findings suggest that the underlying principles are shared across species of varying complexity.

title: Persistent impairment of spatial hearing and neural binaural interaction after “temporary” noise-induced hearing loss
abstract: Many people have suprathreshold auditory processing difficulties despite normal audiometric thresholds, referred to as “hidden hearing loss.” Such difficulties are widely thought to originate from pathology of the inner hair cell ribbon synapse (cochlear synaptopathy) following noise-exposure-induced temporary threshold shifts. This pathology impairs the temporally-precise sound encoding necessary for spatial hearing, but direct evidence in primates, human or nonhuman, is lacking. Here, we show in macaques of both sexes that noise-exposure-induced temporary threshold shifts produced long-lasting alterations in synaptic morphology without synapse loss, and persistent spatial hearing deficits up to 11 months post-exposure, despite recovery of audiometric thresholds. These deficits were accompanied by a reduction in a neurophysiological measure of binaural processing - the binaural interaction component of the auditory brainstem response. Together, these findings provide evidence, in primates, that noise exposure disrupts spatial hearing and binaural neural circuit function without loss of hair cells or synapses.

title: KCNQ1 disruption alters human neuronal development through mitochondrial and insulin signalling pathways
abstract: KCNQ1 encodes a voltage-gated potassium channel implicated in peripheral and neurological disorders, but its role in human neurodevelopment remains unclear. We generated KCNQ1 knockout (KO) human induced pluripotent stem cells and differentiated them into neural stem cells (NSCs) and cortical neurons. KCNQ1 -deficient NSCs show impaired neurite outgrowth, linked to reduced cell adhesion and disrupted neural cell adhesion molecule signalling, a phenotype reproduced by pharmacological KCNQ1 inhibition. Multi-omics and follow-up analyses reveal mitochondrial dysfunction, including reduced mitochondrial copy number and ATP synthase expression. KO cells also show impaired insulin signalling, with diminished insulin receptor gene expression and altered RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT pathways. In differentiated neuronal cultures, KCNQ1 loss decreases synaptic activity and maintains an immature transcriptional profile. Together, these findings identify a role for KCNQ1 in regulating cell adhesion, mitochondrial function, insulin signalling, and neuronal maturation, expanding our understanding of processes that may contribute to neurological manifestations associated with KCNQ1 -related disorders.
keywords: Ion channels in the nervous system

title: Divergent processing strategies for auditory sequence recognition in humans and zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata)
abstract: Deriving sequential information from complex sounds is a challenge for auditory systems, yet it remains unclear whether humans and nonhuman species integrate multidimensional cues or prioritize a single dimension when processing multidimensional input. We investigated how humans and zebra finches ( Taeniopygia guttata ) process concurrent acoustic cues using an identical behavioural paradigm with complex-tone sequences. By presenting probe stimuli that selectively preserved or disrupted either pitch or formant trajectory, we quantified these processing strategies. We show that zebra finches employ an additive integration strategy, treating pitch and formant trajectories as complementary components of a unified auditory pattern. In contrast, humans exhibit a dominant reliance on pitch. Experience further modulates this bias, with trained human listeners recruiting secondary cues to preserve learned relational structure when pitch is unreliable. These findings imply a cross-species divergence in auditory representation, suggesting that auditory processing is shaped by an interplay of species-specific priorities and experience-dependent functional substitution.

title: Functional specialization and dynamical interaction in human amygdala subregions support fearful-expression processing
abstract: Fearful-expression processing supports adaptive responses to potential threats, requiring both rapid threat evaluation and face-related information processing. However, how human amygdala subregions contribute to these complementary processes remains unclear. Here we record intracranial electroencephalography from twelve patients with epilepsy during an emotional face-matching task, sampling 58 amygdala contacts with balanced hemispheric distributions. Condition-specific analyses reveal separable theta/alpha dynamics between the lateral and medial amygdala within fearful-face and neutral-face matching conditions, but not shape matching. Between-condition contrasts further reveal earlier lateral amygdala engagement and stronger lateral-to-medial directional interactions for fearful-face versus neutral-face matching, whereas later medial engagement and stronger medial-to-lateral interactions emerge for neutral-face versus shape matching. Control analyses preserve the main neural effects. In a separate cohort of seven patients, intracranial stimulation produces dissociable behavioral effects, with lateral stimulation impairing fear matching and medial stimulation facilitating neutral-face matching. Together, these findings reveal a condition-dependent functional differentiation within the human amygdala during fearful-expression processing.

title: CircAbcc1-encoded ABCC1-677aa modulates DLX1 to suppress ferroptosis in chronic cerebral ischemia
abstract: Cerebral ischemia leads to progressive neurological dysfunction due to restricted blood perfusion in the brain. While circular RNAs are known to regulate pathological processes, their ability to encode functional proteins during ischemic injury remains unclear. Here, we show that the circular RNA circAbcc1 suppresses ferroptosis in mouse and cellular models of chronic cerebral ischemia‘. We found that circAbcc1 translates into a functional protein, ABCC1-677aa. This protein actively interacts with and phosphorylates the transcription factor DLX1, triggering its export from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. This translocation prevents DLX1 from transcriptionally repressing the crucial anti-ferroptotic genes, Gpx4 and Fsp1 . The subsequent upregulation of Gpx4 and Fsp1 limits lipid peroxidation and iron accumulation, successfully protecting brain neurons from ferroptosis. These findings elucidate a regulatory mechanism driven by a circular RNA-encoded protein and identify the circAbcc1-DLX1 axis as a potential therapeutic target for cerebral ischemic injury.
keywords: Cell death in the nervous system

title: Uncoupling of seagrass host selection and succession for microbial guilds in meadow chronosequence
abstract: Succession describes the predictable assembly of communities and habitats towards increasingly complex ecosystems. In marine meadows, the relative roles of succession and host selection in structuring microbial communities and functions remain unclear. Using chronosequences of the pioneering seagrass Halophila ovalis , we examined bacterial community succession (16S rRNA gene) and functional genes linked to nitrogen fixation and sulfur cycling ( nifH , soxB , aprA , dsrA ) across meadow sediments and seagrass microbiomes (rhizoplane and phylloplane). Sediment communities diversified progressively with distance from the patch edge, whereas host-associated microbiomes were differentially impacted from the meadow sediments, indicating strong host selection. For sulfur-cycling genes, taxonomic succession was decoupled from gene-sequence diversity, while only nifH exhibited successional patterns. Nevertheless, all communities displayed directional assembly trajectories despite being shaped by contrasting ecological processes. Our findings show that both succession and host selection predictably drive microbial community assembly in developing seagrass meadows, while functional gene potential responded in a niche-dependent manner.

title: Selective inhibition of IL-6 trans-signalling reveals distinct mechanisms of human classic and trans-signalling receptor-complex formation
abstract: The cytokine interleukin-6 orchestrates inflammation through two distinct pathways of receptor activation: anti-inflammatory classic signalling via membrane-bound interleukin-6 receptor and pro-inflammatory trans-signalling via soluble interleukin-6 receptor. Current interleukin-6-targeted therapies block both pathways, thereby disrupting essential homeostatic functions initiated by classic signalling. We here show a high-affinity, human-specific antibody that selectively inhibits interleukin-6 trans-signalling. This antibody maintains classic signalling-induced expression of hepatic acute phase genes while completely blocking trans-signalling-induced activation of endothelial cells. By targeting the domain D2 of membrane-bound and soluble human interleukin-6 receptor, the antibody selectively prevents formation of the trans-signalling receptor complex without interfering with ligand binding. This selective blockade demonstrates that human interleukin-6 classic and trans-signalling proceed through distinct receptor assemblies. Our findings describe mechanistic insight into interleukin-6 receptor assembly and provide a strategy to suppress inflammatory interleukin-6 activity while preserving regenerative and anti-inflammatory signalling, thus offering both conceptual and potential therapeutic advances in the targeted modulation of cytokine signalling networks.

title: NEDD1 stabilization regulated by hUTP14a and FBW7γ axis safeguards mitotic cell fate homeostasis
abstract: Accurate spindle formation is vital for mitotic progression and genomic DNA segregation, with γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) mediating microtubule nucleation, and NEDD1 serving as its essential recruitment/anchoring adaptor. However, the mechanisms underlying the regulation of NEDD1 remain largely elusive. Here, we identify a pathway that controls NEDD1 stability during mitosis. hUTP14a relocates to the perichromosomal region at mitotic onset; its depletion causes mitotic catastrophe, impaired chromosomal congression, and reduced γ-tubulin recruitment around chromosomes. Mass spectrometry identifies NEDD1 as a critical hUTP14a-interacting partner during mitosis. hUTP14a protects NEDD1 from ubiquitin-mediated degradation. UbiBrowser 2.0 database prediction and validation experiments identify FBW7γ as an E3 ligase to promote NEDD1 K323 ubiquitination-mediated degradation, while hUTP14a facilitates FBW7γ degradation in a leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-dependent manner. The hUTP14a depletion-induced mitotic catastrophe is reversed by ectopic Flag-NEDD1-K323R but not wild-type Flag-NEDD1. Thus, NEDD1 is stabilized via hUTP14a-mediated FBW7γ degradation to safeguard mitotic cell fate.

title: Engineering T cell-selective chemokine inhibitors through network-level directed evolution
abstract: Immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) are sustained by chemokine-driven recruitment of effector T cells. Although direct suppression of T cell function can be effective, systemic immunosuppression and infection risk limit clinical utility. Targeting chemokine networks offers an alternative strategy, yet chemokine redundancy has hindered the development of clinically effective inhibitors. Tick evasins overcome chemokine redundancy by binding multiple chemokines. Here we show that network-level directed evolution of class B evasin-derived peptides generates T cell-selective chemokine inhibitors. In contrast to analogous class A-derived peptides, these preferentially bind and inhibit chemokines that drive T cell migration. Structural modelling of chemokine:peptide complexes and structure-guided mutagenesis suggest that evasin-derived peptides sterically occlude receptor-binding surfaces and that class B-derived peptides exhibit a more compact organisation of key interaction hotspots than a previously characterised class A-derived peptide. Together, these findings suggest that anti-chemokine peptide specificity can be engineered through scaffold choice and network-level directed evolution.

title: Conserved Core but Divergent Biochemical Features of RAS-MAPK Signalling in C. elegans
abstract: Genetic studies in Caenorhabditis elegans have established core principles of RAS-MAPK signalling. These nematodes encode three RAS proteins: LET-60/KRAS is essential for vulval induction, while RAS-1 and RAS-2 are orthologs of RRAS/RRAS2 and MRAS, respectively, but remain biologically and biochemically uncharacterized. We here present a comprehensive biochemical analysis of all three C. elegans RAS proteins, defining nucleotide cycling and effector interactions. We show that conserved RAS scaffolds are tuned by sequence variation to balance signalling with developmental fidelity. LET-60 has significantly impaired nucleotide exchange and changing its sequence to match human KRAS induces a protruding vulva phenotype in vivo. RAS-1 rapidly exchanges GDP-to-GTP, whereas RAS-2 remains consistently GDP-bound. LET-60 engages the RAF ortholog LIN-45 through a divergent interface, and RAS-1 unexpectedly drives SOC-2:RAS:PP1C holophosphatase assembly in a nucleotide-independent manner. Our findings reveal both conserved and distinctive biochemical features underlying RAS signalling and suggest species-specific tuning of this key proliferation pathway.

title: Age-related shift towards feedforward motor control under uncertainty
abstract: Humans perform movements in the face of uncertainty on a daily basis. To accomplish these tasks without error, young adults frequently rely on feedback-mediated motor strategies that allow them to update their movement as uncertainty evolves. However, it remains unclear how aging impacts the ability to plan and execute movement under uncertain conditions. Here we use a “go-before-you-know” pointing task completed during functional neuroimaging to examine how aging influences movement planning under uncertainty. Behaviorally, young adults employed a strategy consistent with feedback-mediated control, biasing their trajectories toward the more likely target when uncertainty was low, and intermediate to potential targets when uncertainty was high. Older adults employed a different approach, shifting away from an intermediate reaching strategy, particularly under high uncertainty, suggesting a shift toward feedforward control. Neuroimaging mirrored these behavioral patterns, revealing that young adults encoded task uncertainty and movement direction in sensorimotor regions more strongly than older adults. Overall, these findings suggest that aging diminishes the ability to flexibly encode task-related uncertainty, leading to a shift towards feedforward control strategies.

title: Distinct genetic perturbations at the endogenous Atf4 locus uncouple polyadenylation loss from transcriptional readthrough
abstract: Transcription termination by RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) is coupled to co-transcriptional cleavage and polyadenylation directed by the canonical AAUAAA polyadenylation signal (PAS). However, the in vivo requirement of the canonical PAS for termination fidelity remains unclear. Here, we dissect PAS-dependent termination at the endogenous Atf4 locus using complementary mouse models. A previously characterized Atf4 ΔCDS + ΔPAS allele deleting exons 2-3 induces strong transcriptional readthrough, producing an Atf4 – Cacna1i fusion transcript that suppresses Rps19bp1 and causes severe cardiac defects. To isolate PAS function, we generated an Atf4 ΔCDS allele retaining the PAS and an Atf4 ΔPAS allele preserving the coding sequence but deleting the PAS. The ΔCDS allele produces modest readthrough, whereas ΔPAS does not produce detectable downstream readthrough. Instead, PAS loss permits utilization of a cryptic intragenic polyadenylation site within exon 3, generating a prematurely terminated transcript. These findings demonstrate that PAS loss does not necessarily cause transcriptional readthrough in vivo and can instead promote alternative polyadenylation at an endogenous mammalian locus.

title: Towards a unified biology of vertebrate number sense
abstract: Number sense, the ability to estimate and compare numerical quantities, emerges early in development and is widespread across species. Despite decades of work on behavioural and neural correlates of numerosity, the genetic and mechanistic foundations remain poorly integrated. We propose a review and perspective that brings together evidence from vertebrates. Our unique focus relies on how genetic variation, brain lateralisation, and neural circuit organisation across development shape number cognition. We highlight zebrafish ( Danio rerio ) and chicks ( Gallus gallus ) as complementary comparative models that can uncover conserved principles and novel mechanisms, opening new avenues for studying the biological bases of numerical cognition and its disorders from the very early developmental stages.

title: Spi1 and Usp7 aggravate diabetic encephalopathy through regulating Ddx3x
abstract: DEAD-box helicase 3 X-linked (DDX3X) can interact with NOD-like receptor protein 3 (NLRP3) to drive inflammasome activation. Nonetheless, the role of DDX3X on NLRP3 inflammasome activation in diabetic encephalopathy remains unidentified. Here, Ddx3x knockdown alleviates microglial NLRP3 activation, which reverses the increased permeability and decreased tight junction proteins induced by conditioned medium of lipopolysaccharide-stimulated microglia (LPS-CM) in bEnd.3 endothelial cells, and overturns LPS-CM-elicited apoptosis promotion in HT22 neurons. In male type 2 diabetes db/db mice, Ddx3x silencing mitigates microglial activation, blood-brain barrier disruption, neuronal apoptosis and cognitive impairment. Spi-1 proto-oncogene (SPI1) transcriptionally activates Ddx3x ; Additionally, ubiquitin-specific protease (USP)7 reduces DDX3X ubiquitination to increase its protein stability. Silencing Spi1 / Usp7 exerts beneficial effects in vitro and in vivo, which are neutralized when overexpressing Ddx3x . In conclusion, Spi1 / Usp7 knockdown downregulates DDX3X to inhibit microglial NLRP3 activation, alleviating BBB dysfunction and neuronal loss to ameliorate diabetic encephalopathy, which suggests prospective targets for diabetic encephalopathy.

title: Evolutionary transitions in social organization and the relationship between climate and queen number in ant societies
abstract: In about one fourth of ant species, multiple queens reproduce within the same colony (‘polygyny’), reducing relatedness and potentially fuelling evolutionary conflicts among colony members. Polygyny is more common at higher altitudes / latitudes in several species, suggesting that cold climates favour multiple queens. We tested this prediction with phylogenetic analyses comparing 263 ant species and modelled the evolutionary pathways between alternative social structures. Queen number was phylogenetically labile, with bidirectional transitions between single and multi-queen species passing through socially polymorphic species (with both types of colonies). Contrary to our predictions, polygyny was not more common at higher latitudes or altitudes. Socially polymorphic species tended to occur in environments with more uniform precipitation throughout the year, and queen number increased towards the tropics. We discuss how multiple queening may be favoured in warm climates due to competitive advantages of faster colony growth and higher genetic diversity. We also call for more studies in tropical regions, as most studies were performed in the northern hemisphere.

title: Flippability of Escherichia coli membrane proteins under lipid stress reveals a new job for old genes
abstract: Normally, the “flip-flop” motion is reserved for small lipid molecules which move from one leaflet of the membrane to the other, and even that process is very slow without the aid of specific enzymes. Unexpectedly, we recently found that despite a prohibitively high energy barrier, Escherichia coli cardiolipin (CL) synthase A (ClsA) flips its large catalytic domain across the inner (cytoplasmic) membrane (IM) when cells were fully or partially depleted of phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and that this was necessary to support cell viability. Here, we demonstrated that production of the non-native phospholipid phosphatidylcholine (PC) in PE-depleted cells prevents ClsA flipping and halts cell growth, a phenotype rescued by constitutively inverted ClsA. Surprisingly, properly oriented lactose permease (LacY) acts as a multicopy suppressor, rescuing the growth defect in the -PE+PC cells. These data indicate that neutral PC regulates the membrane topology of ClsA and LacY, and subsequently the appearance of CL to the periplasmic leaflet required for viability. Therefore, ClsA and potentially LacY may achieve varied roles from the same amino acid sequence through an unusual flip-flopping mechanism. This fruitful “repurposing” of genetic material highlights the remarkable adaptability of living organisms and their membranes.

title: The representation of order and randomness in the auditory cortex
abstract: Perception fundamentally relies on the brain’s ability to extract structure from its sensory environment. The auditory cortex possesses significant sensitivity to statistical regularities in tone sequences. To examine this phenomenon at the single-neuron level, we used multitone sequences and recorded responses from the auditory cortex of awake adult female Sprague Dawley rats. Tones were presented in periodic sequences with a fixed, repeated cycle; in a fully random condition; or in an intermediate condition in which cycles were maintained, but tones were randomly permuted within each cycle (random cycle condition). Units showed a continuum of preferences between order-preferring neurons and randomness-preferring neurons. Unexpectedly, we found sensitivity to the position of sounds in the cycle (‘phase modulation’). The strongest and most consistent phase modulations were in the responses to the random cycle condition. Finally, we show how such phase sensitivity may emerge from a simple, biologically plausible computation.

title: VASP cooperates with zyxin to organize mechanically competent adhesions
abstract: Focal adhesions (FAs) are dynamic macromolecular assemblies that anchor the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix via integrin receptors, thereby regulating cell morphology and migration. Here, we show that the vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein (VASP) cooperates with the mechanosensitive scaffold protein zyxin to maintain FA during maturation under actomyosin-generated tension. Using sequential CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing and cryo-electron tomography, we resolved the in situ nanoarchitecture of the FA-stress fiber interface. We establish that tropomyosin decorates the dorsal aspect of adhesion-associated stress fibers independently of VASP and zyxin. VASP and zyxin are required for the assembly of dense, aligned actin bundles with uniform polarity, oriented with their barbed ends toward the cell edge. Live-cell imaging and quantitative analyses of cells confined on micropatterns reveal that VASP and zyxin cooperate to preserve the mechanical coupling between FAs and the actin cytoskeleton under contractile load. Our findings establish that VASP and zyxin perform distinct yet complementary functions to organize FA-associated actin into mechanically competent force-transmitting units.

title: BUB signaling in cancer and molecular insights into targeted therapies
abstract: The Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC) is vital for proper chromosome segregation during cell division and for maintaining genomic integrity; its disruption can cause aneuploidy and tumors. The BUB gene family ensures SAC fidelity by regulating kinetochore–microtubule attachments and mitotic progression. Dysregulation leads to chromosomal instability (CIN), contributing to cancer progression, heterogeneity, metastasis, and therapy resistance. Beyond mitosis, BUB proteins influence DNA repair, chromatin remodeling, transcription, and immune responses. They interact with cell cycle and genome stability pathways, impacting cancer prognosis and therapy response. Research is ongoing to validate BUB proteins as biomarkers and develop inhibitors, possibly combined with immunotherapies or DNA-damaging agents for resistant tumors. This review summarizes their functions, highlighting their potential in personalized cancer treatment.

title: A circRNA-microRNA-Pdcd1 axis drives microglial activation and retinal ganglion cell degeneration
abstract: Retinal ganglion cell (RGC) degeneration is the primary cause of vision loss, driven by the complicated effects of intrinsic neuronal damage and neuroinflammation. However, current single-target therapies fail to address these dual pathological challenges. CircRNAs, functioning through ceRNA networks, represent a multi-target intervention due to their stability. Here we show that, using whole‑transcriptome sequencing of optic nerve crush (ONC), we bioinformatically predicted nine candidate ceRNA networks. Among these, the network centered on circAgtpbp1 was significantly up-regulated post-injury, independent of its host gene. Mechanistically, circAgtpbp1 functions as a ceRNA by sequestering miR-3098-3p, thereby de-repressing the translation of PD-1 ( Pdcd1 ). In the ONC model, this upregulation of PD-1 protein amplifies microglial activation, creating a pathogenic non-cell-autonomous inflammatory amplification loop that drives RGC degeneration. Our findings not only uncover a novel circRNA-mediated mechanism in neurodegeneration but also identify the circAgtpbp1-miR-3098-3p-Pdcd1-microglia axis as a promising therapeutic target for neuroprotective interventions.

title: Towards a comprehensive landscape and mechanism understanding of virus-disease associations
abstract: Viruses are linked to human diseases through complex molecular mechanisms, yet a comprehensive investigation of virus-disease associations and their molecular basis remains lacking. We curated 3,555 high-confidence virus-disease associations involving 267 viruses and 954 diseases through text-mining over 28 million PubMed abstracts followed by rigorous manual verification, establishing the most comprehensive resource in this field to date. We then developed AVD, a user-friendly online database to store, visualize, and analyze these associations and their molecular mechanisms. Our analysis revealed that virus-disease association patterns are significantly influenced by viral taxonomy, phenotype, and key biological traits such as transmissibility, transmission routes, and tissue tropism. Molecular analysis identified a core set of bridging genes involved in the majority of virus-disease associations. Notably, these bridging genes were extensively involved in viral infections and diseases, and exhibit distinct characteristics, including a high proportion of secreted proteins, elevated expression across human tissues, and high centrality in the human protein-protein interaction network. Furthermore, we developed a machine-learning model capable of accurately predicting virus-disease associations. Collectively, this study provides a valuable data resource and analytical framework for studying virus-disease relationships and offers novel insights into their molecular mechanisms.
keywords: Policy and public health in microbiology

title: Metabolic characteristics and evolutionary history of the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial endosymbionts of pennate diatoms
abstract: Nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria are important sources of bioavailable nitrogen on Earth. Some nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria are endosymbionts of algae, and recently one of them, UCYN-A2, was shown to be an early-stage organelle (nitroplast) of haptophytes. These biological associations are important models for studying co-evolution and organellogenesis. Endosymbioses between Rhopalodiaceae diatoms and nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria (spheroid bodies, SBs) are widespread in marine and freshwater ecosystems, but their adaptation and evolution remain unclear. We found that the genomes and metabolic characteristics of marine and freshwater SBs are remarkably similar. Purifying selection pressures dominated SB diversification both within marine and freshwater habitats and across habitat boundaries. The metabolic characteristics and genome reduction of SBs are substantially different from UCYN-A, suggesting different evolutionary journeys for the endosymbionts influenced by different hosts. We estimated that the marine SBs diversified ~185 Mya (95% highest posterior density (HPD): 340-88 Mya), which was within a prolonged oligotrophic period in the ocean, during which UCYN-A also diversified. The freshwater SBs diversified from the marine SBs ~137 Mya (95% HPD: 258-66 Mya) and further diversified ~80 Mya (95% HPD: 157-31 Mya), when sea level was increasing. Our study reveals the genetic and metabolic underpinnings characterizing the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial endosymbionts of Rhopalodiaceae diatoms.

title: Vascular tree structure-based perfusion phantom fabrication using modified Hele-Shaw cell method
abstract: Tissue phantoms mimicking microvasculature and perfusion are essential for vasculature modelling and calibrating imaging systems, which require faithful replication of vascular geometry and flow. Conventional fabrication methods, including lithographic micromachining and additive manufacturing remain constrained by predefined designs, rectangular channel cross-sections, limited scalability, and high production costs. Here we present a lithography-free approach based on a modified lifted Hele-Shaw cell method where, unlike above-mentioned methods, random fractal-like vascular structures emerge naturally. This results in channels of widths 100-1000 μ m with smooth Gaussian cross-section and natural diameter tapering. We demonstrate this with four phantom designs: a planar vascular tree, a cerebral vasculature-mimicking guided tree network, a conformable curved substrate and a retinal vasculature-mimicking network. Flow visualisation with laser speckle contrast imaging shows close agreement with in vivo observations and consistency with the generalized Murray’s law. This approach uniquely combines fractal-like network formation leading towards realistic vascular geometry and flow characteristics, offering an in vitro alternative to small animal vascular models.

title: FOXO3 induces chromatin changes in a model of DNA damage-induced senescence
abstract: FOXO transcription factors are critical for cellular homeostasis and the stress response and have been implicated in longevity in several species. Yet, how these factors function at the chromatin level in differing conditions in human cells is poorly understood. Here, we take an integrated multi-omics approach to identify the chromatin-level mechanisms by which FOXO3 coordinates transcriptional programs in replicating cells and in a model of cellular senescence. In a DNA-damage induced senescence, FOXO3 levels are elevated early in senescence entry. Increased FOXO3 expression induces expression of chromatin remodeling factors, and impacts chromatin accessibility across the genome together with SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers. As cells enter DNA-damage induced senescence, FOXO3 is essential for chromatin remodeling and reprogramming of a genomic network that functions to modulate cell stress and lineage-specific cellular functions. Altogether, we identify a FOXO3-SWI/SNF network that regulates key cellular processes including metabolism, proteostasis, epigenetics, and cell lineage, and is dynamically controlled under DNA damaging conditions.

title: Large-scale functional overlap between dorsal and ventral object-responsive networks
abstract: The processes of acting on and recognizing objects have traditionally been attributed to dorsal and ventral visual pathways, respectively. Although extensive evidence suggests that the two pathways interact, the extent and the strength of these interactions across whole-brain networks remain unclear. In two experiments, we characterized the whole-brain network connections of object-selective regions in each pathway using functional magnetic resonance imaging data acquired while participants viewed objects. Here, we show substantial spatial overlap in connectivity networks generated from the dorsal and the ventral seed region—with greater similarity between object networks within an individual than each network shows across individuals. This overlap persists across viewing of tools and non-tools and even after controlling for the shared variance between pathways. Together, these findings reveal that dorsal and ventral pathways form highly overlapping and distributed networks in the service of object perception.

title: Estradiol deficiency aggravates AngII-induced vascular remodeling by failing to inhibit GRK2 through ERα-mediated autophagy
abstract: Hypertension acts as a critical cardiovascular risk factor that drives vascular remodeling, which manifests as vascular media thickening triggered by excessive proliferation and migration of vascular smooth muscle cells. Angiotensin II promotes vascular remodeling by upregulating G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2. Estradiol deficiency, particularly among postmenopausal individuals, increases susceptibility to hypertension by overactivating the renin-angiotensin system, while the precise mechanism remains unkown. Here we show that estradiol inhibits G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 to ameliorate hypertensive vascular remodeling. Ovariectomy in spontaneously hypertensive rats exacerbate hypertension, while estradiol supplementation significantly reduced blood pressure and attenuated vascular remodeling. Mechanistically, Estradiol downregulated G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 expression, leading to decreased β-arrestin2 recruitment and ERK signaling, thereby reducing vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation and migration. Additionally, Autophagy or estrogen receptor α blockade abolishes the effects of estradiol on G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 degradation. This study provides a potential therapeutic strategy for hypertensive vascular remodeling.

title: Phospholipid remodeling of the cardiomyocyte membrane affects cardiac function
abstract: Membrane phospholipid (PL) remodeling has been linked to various mammalian metabolic and oncogenic pathologies, but its role in the heart remains elusive. Here, we investigated the role of PL remodeling in cardiac function. Lysophospholipid acyltransferase 7 (LPLAT7)/lysophosphatidylglycerol acyltransferase 1 (LPGAT1) remodels phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), two major cardiac membrane PL species. Public functional genomics data revealed downregulation of LPLAT7/LPGAT1 gene expression in failing human hearts and murine cardiomyocytes. Cardiomyocyte-specific Lplat7/Lpgat1 -deficient male mice exhibited selective remodeling of cardiac PC and PE composition, including diminished stearic acid- and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA)-enriched species. LPLAT7/LPGAT1 suppression induced myocardial contractile dysfunction associated with cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) activation and abnormal calcium handling, partially rescued by pharmacological PKA inhibition. Conversely, Lplat7/Lpgat1 overexpression partially improved pressure overload-induced cardiac dysfunction with selective restoration of PC(40:6), a major stearic acid/DHA-enriched PC species. These findings highlight the contributory role of LPLAT7/LPGAT1-dependent membrane PL remodeling in cardiac function and heart failure.

title: A Colletotrichum orbiculare-based fungal model recapitulates conserved cellular defects of Niemann–Pick type C disease and enables therapeutic evaluation
abstract: Niemann–Pick type C disease is a fatal lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in NPC1 or NPC2 , leading to lipid accumulation and progressive neurodegeneration. Current mammalian models recapitulate major pathological features but are limited by long disease courses and low throughput. Here, we establish the plant-pathogenic fungus Colletotrichum orbiculare as a scalable eukaryotic model of Niemann–Pick type C disease. Introduction of disease-associated mutations into fungal NPC1 or NPC2 homologs abolishes pathogenicity, showing that NPC dysfunction compromises lipid-dependent morphogenesis required for host penetration. Conversely, human NPC1 partially restores fungal infection. Together, these findings support functional conservation of NPC-dependent cellular processes across kingdoms. Miglustat and 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin restore pathogenicity through distinct lipid pathways. These complementary modes of rescue indicate that NPC1 and NPC2 dysfunction converges on lipid-dependent morphogenesis closely linked to actin organization. By connecting lipid metabolism, actin organization, and pharmacological rescue to a measurable infection outcome, this fungal model provides a tractable and scalable platform for mechanistic and therapeutic exploration.

title: Organelle associations and metabolic rewiring of size-defined hepatic lipid droplets
abstract: Lipid droplet (LD) size is a key determinant of hepatic lipid metabolism, yet the molecular programming routing size-defined subpopulations to distinct fates remains unclear. Here we show that a fractionation workflow resolves hepatic LDs by size and organelle association, defining a high-confidence intrinsic LD proteome. Moreover, comparative proteomics of fasted livers reveals a clear ‘division of labor’: Large LDs (L-LDs) function as specialized mitochondrion-coupled ‘putative fueling hubs’, whereas small LDs (S-LDs) serve as lysosome-coupled ‘putative trafficking and turnover hubs’. This interaction map is highly plastic; metabolic stress (fasting or steatosis) triggers a programmatic remodeling where lysosomal machinery is inducibly recruited to S-LDs. Crucially, in vivo stress recruits mitochondria to both pools, supporting a ‘parallel programs’ model where S-LD-associated mitochondria are hypothesized to power the energy-intensive degradative machinery. These findings establish that metabolic state leverages LD size to direct organelle partnerships, nominating the small-LD lysosomal axis as a critical regulatory node in metabolic-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD).

title: Inhibition of DCLK1 promotes spinal cord injury recovery: implications for KATNA1 phosphorylation in microtubule-dependent neurite outgrowth
abstract: Functional recovery after spinal cord injury (SCI) remains challenging, requiring therapeutic targets. Here, we show that doublecortin-like kinase 1 (DCLK1) is upregulated after SCI in mice. Pharmacological inhibition of DCLK1 with DCLK1-IN-1 improved motor recovery, reduced glial scar formation and fibrosis, and preserved neurons at the lesion site. Mechanistically, we identified the microtubule-severing protein KATNA1 as a downstream target of DCLK1. DCLK1 directly phosphorylated KATNA1 at threonine 118 (T118), suppressing its microtubule-severing activity. DCLK1 overexpression inhibited, whereas DCLK1 knockdown or inhibition enhanced KATNA1 function. The T118D mutation reduced KATNA1 activity, while T118A resisted DCLK1-mediated suppression. In neurons, DCLK1 inhibited KATNA1-induced neurite outgrowth, whereas DCLK1 inhibition restored this effect. Together, these results identify DCLK1 as a promising therapeutic target for SCI and reveal a mechanism by which DCLK1 regulates KATNA1 phosphorylation to modulate microtubule severing and neurite outgrowth.

title: Standardizing deoxygenation studies in coral biology
abstract: Deoxygenation, the global loss of biologically available oxygen (O 2 ) from the world’s oceans, presents a pervasive and intensifying threat for reef-building corals that will require coordinated efforts to understand and manage. However, recent expansion of coral deoxygenation experimentation has produced methodological gaps, limiting collective knowledge generation. Here, we show that growing divergence in this field arises primarily from differences in focal phenotypes, deoxygenation exposures, and experimental execution that together prevent biological from technical variation from being disentangled between studies. To address this, we propose a series of recommendations to establish the foundation for a future standardized framework for coral deoxygenation methodology. Such efforts are critical to establish a robust consensus of scientific data to support effective management of reef deoxygenation. Waiting decades for diverging methodologies to prompt a call for standardization may be imprudent given the urgent threat of deoxygenation and the abundant methodological divergence present in coral deoxygenation experimentation.

title: SGLT2 inhibitors attenuate diabetic kidney disease by suppressing YAP dependent ferroptosis
abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors provide renal protection in diabetic kidney disease (DKD) through mechanisms beyond glucose lowering, but these remain incompletely understood. Here we show that Yes-associated protein 1 (YAP)-dependent ferroptosis contributes to renal tubular injury in DKD and that suppression of this pathway underlies part of the renoprotective effects of dapagliflozin. In human DKD kidney tissues, nuclear YAP accumulation correlates positively with ferroptosis markers acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) and 4-hydroxynonenal, and negatively with renal function. In a diabetic rat model, dapagliflozin attenuates renal dysfunction, tubular injury, and fibrosis alongside reduced YAP activation and ferroptosis. In high-glucose-treated renal tubular epithelial cells, YAP promotes nuclear translocation, upregulates ACSL4 and transferrin receptor expression, induces iron accumulation and mitochondrial damage, and drives ferroptotic cell death. YAP knockdown and pharmacological inhibition both confirm an upstream regulatory role for YAP in ferroptosis. Mechanistically, YAP and TEAD4 enhance ACSL4 promoter activity through a conserved TEAD-binding motif, an effect suppressed by dapagliflozin. These findings identify the YAP/TEAD4-ACSL4 axis as a therapeutic target underlying glucose-independent renoprotection by SGLT2 inhibition.

title: Integrating corneal endophenotypes with classic GWAS approaches identifies novel keratoconus loci
authors: Frank J. H. M. van den Biggelaar
Carla J. H. van der Kallen
Frank C. T. van der Heide
abstract: Keratoconus is a chronic progressive disorder characterized by corneal deformation. It usually affects adolescents and young adults, reducing vision and decreasing the quality of life. Here we show that integrating genetic analyses of corneal traits with large case-control studies improves the discovery and annotation of genetic factors underlying keratoconus. Analysing corneal imaging measurements from 16,464 individuals, we identify four informative corneal traits and use them in a multi-trait genetic analysis that uncovers 80 significant loci associated with one or more of the selected traits. Twenty-five of these loci (5 novel) are also associated with keratoconus (Bonferroni-corrected P ≤ 6.3 × 10 −4 ). A subsequent meta-analysis of 6,372 cases and 593,541 controls identifies 51 significant keratoconus loci ( P ≤ 5.0 × 10 −8 ), including eight not previously reported. Gene-set analysis implicates pathways involved in extracellular matrix integrity, glucosylceramidase regulation and cellular differentiation. These findings expand the genetic landscape of keratoconus, provide insight into the biological mechanisms underlying disease development, and support future efforts in genetic risk profiling and therapeutic target discovery.

title: Chronic XBP1s signaling promotes B cell dysfunction and anergy
abstract: B cells are central mediators of humoral immunity, and their development is tightly regulated to prevent autoreactivity. The unfolded protein response (UPR) plays a crucial role in supporting the high biosynthetic demands of B cells.
